title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill
openingText: The subject of this Essay is not what is called Liberty of the Will, so unfortunately set against the misleadingly named doctrine of Philosophical Necessity. It is Civil, or Social Liberty: the nature and limits of the power that society may legitimately exercise over an individual. This question is seldom formulated, and scarcely ever discussed, in general terms. Yet its unacknowledged presence deeply influences the practical disputes of our age, and it will probably soon be recognised as the vital question of the future. Far from being new, it has in a sense divided humanity from almost the earliest times. But at the stage of progress now reached by the more civilised parts of the human race, the question arises under new conditions and calls for a different and more fundamental examination.
about:
On Liberty asks when society may rightly compel an individual to act or refrain from acting. Mill argues that preventing harm to others can justify coercion, while a competent adult's own good is not enough. He distinguishes legal penalties from the pressure of public opinion, and defends freedom of discussion, individual character and different ways of living. His examples also show that harm does not automatically justify intervention.

Published in 1859, the book opens with a dedication to Mill's late wife and intellectual partner. He describes the work as belonging as much to her as to him, while regretting that she could not complete her review of it. The argument addresses the political and religious disputes of his time, including majority opinion, education, temperance campaigns and the growth of state administration.

The five chapters move from a statement of the principle to discussion, individuality, society's authority and practical applications. Read the qualifications as carefully as the memorable claims. Mill excludes children from his adult freedom principle and makes a troubling exception for peoples he calls 'barbarians'. His defence of liberty and his assumptions about who is ready for it need to be examined together.

angleCards.title: When does harm justify intervention?
angleCards.text: Distinguish harm from offence and from the losses that legitimate competition causes. In chapter 5, Mill explicitly says that harm can be a necessary ground for intervention without always being sufficient.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to test Mill's harm principle against his examples, paying attention to risk, obligations to others and the difference between a necessary and a sufficient reason for coercion.

angleCards.title: Why does individuality matter?
angleCards.text: Chapter 3 defends different ways of living both for the people who choose them and for those who may learn from them. Mill also gives ordinary people, not only geniuses, a claim to choose their own lives.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine why Mill values individuality, how it benefits others and where his defence depends on assumptions about human development.

angleCards.title: What can disagreement teach us?
angleCards.text: A suppressed opinion may be true or partly true. Even a false opinion can make others understand the grounds of their beliefs. Follow the distinction between an inherited formula and a conviction someone can defend.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace Mill's different arguments for open discussion and test his claim that understanding a view requires seriously engaging with its opponents.

angleCards.title: Who receives the promised freedom?
angleCards.text: Mill's exception for peoples he calls 'barbarians' sits uneasily beside his defence of self-development. His discussions of marriage, children and Mormonism offer further tests of consent, power and the freedom to leave.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine the exclusions and tensions in Mill's account of liberty, distinguishing his historical assumptions from the principles he argues for.

cast.name: John Stuart Mill
cast.description: Mill argues for limits on both government coercion and social pressure. His stated foundation is utility in its broad sense, grounded in the lasting interests of human beings as developing creatures.

cast.name: Harriet Taylor Mill
cast.description: The dedication commemorates Mill's wife and credits her with inspiring and partly writing the best of his work. He says this book belongs equally to her, while noting that important passages never received her final review.

cast.name: The harm principle
cast.description: Preventing harm to others can justify coercion. A competent adult's own good, or other people's dislike of a choice, is not by itself enough. Mill examines specific duties, risks and exceptions rather than treating every adverse consequence alike.

cast.name: The tyranny of the majority
cast.description: A majority can impose its preferences through public opinion as well as law. Mill asks how to distinguish legitimate criticism and personal choice of company from attempts to punish harmless differences.

cast.name: Wilhelm von Humboldt
cast.description: Mill quotes Humboldt on the development of human capacities through freedom and varied circumstances. He also discusses Humboldt's views on personal agreements, including marriage, and adds qualifications about obligations to others.

cast.name: The conformist
cast.description: This person lets custom decide how to live and rarely exercises independent judgment. Mill uses the figure to explain why even respectable habits can weaken character when they are followed without reflection.

whyItMatters.title: A test for coercion
whyItMatters.body: The book gives readers a way to ask what justifies interference: harm to another person, a specific obligation, a risk, or merely disapproval? Its practical cases expose the difficulty of drawing that boundary. The chapter on applications distinguishes preventing harm from guaranteeing that nobody ever suffers a loss.

whyItMatters.title: Belief needs understanding
whyItMatters.body: Mill asks what happens when a true belief is no longer questioned. A person may keep its words while losing its meaning and reasons. His defence of discussion therefore concerns the education of the listener as well as the freedom of the speaker.

whyItMatters.title: Freedom beyond government
whyItMatters.body: Legal permission does not by itself protect a different way of life. Social pressure can discourage people from thinking and choosing for themselves. Mill's account invites readers to examine both coercive conformity and the legitimate freedom to criticise, advise and choose one's own associations.
